title: Where Have All the Gordon Davises Gone?
author: Aaron M. Renn
summary: Aaron Renn extends his recurring theme of declining leadership in America by passing along Andrew Manshel's reflections on the death of New York parks commissioner Gordon J. Davis. Manshel argues that the elites who rescued Bryant Park in the 1980s and 90s served out of a disinterested commitment to the public interest, and that he cannot name comparable figures among baby boomers. Renn adds that those leaders also had their shoulder to the wheel rather than merely attending galas, and that today's CEOs of global firms have largely delegated civic involvement to regional or government-relations staff. He grants that market pressure and the changed nature of banks explain part of the shift, but concludes that civic organizations have been hollowed out as risk-averse representatives and lobbyists replaced public-spirited elites.
points: Mid-century civic leaders served because they judged the work necessary, not for attention, position, or money, and they personally drove projects forward.
Leaders of global institutions now treat local civic life as a delegated function, which weakens the cities that host their headquarters.
Market pressure and corporate consolidation explain part of the change but not the entire decline in civic engagement.
Civic organizations decay when boards fill with risk-averse regional vice presidents and lobbyists instead of public-spirited elites.
quotes: They were involved in the civic life of New York City because they thought it was important and necessary, not because they were seeking attention, position or money for themselves.
While he only hints at it, in that era figures like these didn’t just sit on boards and go to gala dinners, they also had their shoulder to the wheel, personally helping drive these projects forward.

Relentless market pressures also make it harder for CEOs to devote too much time to civic affairs, or to make many non-market decisions with the firm’s money in order to benefit a particular local market.

Still, there’s no doubt that corporate leaders are not what they used to be in the civic space. Tier 1 type companies have mostly delegated civic involvement to regional leaders or community/government relations people.
Those people no longer populate boards. Rather, they are populated by those regional VP or government relations types, people who are highly risk averse.
We’ve seen a major decline in disinterested leadership, of civic involvement generally, and of the effectiveness of institutions. Similar trends are evident at the national level as well.
One of my recurring themes is the decline of leadership in America, both at the national level and in our communities.
